passage: Biochemists in the Okonkwo laboratory characterized alcohol dehydrogenase purified from a bacterial expression system, focusing on its response to a candidate small-molecule inhibitor designed to resemble acetaldehyde. Reactions contained a fixed enzyme concentration in buffered solution at 25 °C, and initial velocities were measured at six acetaldehyde concentrations with and without 60 µM inhibitor. Product formation was followed spectrophotometrically for the first 60 seconds, a window in which less than 5% of substrate was consumed. Each velocity represents the mean of three independent reactions, and the standard error was below 4% of every mean. The team wished to determine whether the compound binds the free enzyme at the active site or instead binds elsewhere, and to estimate its dissociation constant for the enzyme–inhibitor complex before testing it in cultured cells. Enzyme purity exceeded 95% by SDS-PAGE, and the buffer contained no metal chelators or reducing agents that could interfere with the assay. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

questions.stem: According to Table 1, what is the initial velocity in the presence of inhibitor when [S] = 200 µM?
questions.explanation: Reading the inhibitor column at [S] = 200 µM gives 50 µmol/min; the control column value (100) is the uninhibited rate.
questions.trap: Reading the velocity from the wrong column (control versus inhibitor) or from a neighboring [S] row of Table 1.

questions.stem: Which additional experiment would best distinguish competitive from noncompetitive inhibition by this compound?

options.A: Repeat the assay at a lower temperature to see whether inhibition disappears
options.B: Measure whether very high substrate concentrations restore the uninhibited maximal velocity
options.C: Measure velocity at a single substrate concentration with several enzyme concentrations
options.D: Measure product formation after 60 minutes rather than 60 seconds

questions.explanation: A competitive inhibitor raises apparent Km but leaves Vmax unchanged, so sufficiently high [S] outcompetes it. A noncompetitive inhibitor lowers Vmax regardless of [S].
questions.trap: Choosing an experiment that does not vary substrate concentration, which is what distinguishes competitive from noncompetitive inhibition.

questions.stem: Assuming simple competitive inhibition, what is the approximate Ki of the inhibitor?
questions.explanation: Km,app = Km(1 + [I]/Ki). Here Km,app/Km = 4, so [I]/Ki = 3 and Ki = 60/3 = 20 µM.
questions.trap: Using [I]/α or [I]·α instead of Ki = [I]/(α − 1), where α = Km,app/Km.

questions.stem: Which statement about the data is NOT consistent with competitive inhibition?

options.A: The apparent Km is larger in the presence of the inhibitor
options.B: The inhibitor binds the free enzyme in preference to the enzyme–substrate complex
options.C: The inhibition is weaker at higher substrate concentrations
options.D: Vmax is lower in the presence of the inhibitor at saturating [S]

questions.explanation: Competitive inhibitors leave Vmax unchanged; the velocities converge as [S] rises. A reduced Vmax would indicate noncompetitive or uncompetitive behavior.
questions.trap: Believing any inhibitor that slows the reaction must lower Vmax; a competitive inhibitor only raises apparent Km, so velocities converge toward the same Vmax at high substrate.

questions.stem: Many drugs, such as statins and methotrexate, act as competitive inhibitors. Which property of such drugs most directly explains why they are often structural analogs of the substrate?

options.A: They must lower the enzyme's turnover number at saturating substrate
options.B: They must bind the enzyme–substrate complex only
options.C: They must bind covalently to the enzyme
options.D: They must occupy the same active site as the substrate

questions.explanation: Competition requires binding to the same site; structural similarity to the substrate (or transition state) lets the drug fit the active site and compete reversibly.
questions.trap: Assuming a competitive inhibitor must bind covalently or only the enzyme–substrate complex; it competes with substrate for the active site.
